<reason>Both sides were sharp, disciplined, and closed-book-clean, with no fake sourcing on either side. A built the more inventive case — disclosure as notice-and-consent theatre, the "certificate of regularity" shield, Goodhart-driven metric crudification, and legislative crowd-out — and landed one genuinely damaging hit: after B conceded fraud-threshold exemptions, A showed that B's flagship deactivated driver learns only what he already knew while the decisive thresholds stay hidden (B's closing never answered this). But A's whole route to victory rests on two contested planks that B attacked structurally rather than rhetorically. First, the crowd-out claim: B's Q1 ("what in the motion prevents passing both?") forced A to concede the text permits both, reducing the objection to an unverifiable prediction about who holds the legislative pen — plausible political economy, but it argues "disclosure is insufficient," not "disclosure should not be required," which is the motion as written. Second, B's precondition argument survived: entry powers locate the door but not what is behind it; pattern and discrimination claims need the practice named; a tribunal probing an algorithmic decision presupposes knowing an algorithm decided. A's best counter — a cause standard shifts the burden so secrecy is fatal to the firm — works well for the individual dismissal but leaves B's systemic/prospective auditing advantage largely intact. B also opened with the cleanest decision rule ("may a career-ending system operate invisibly?") and correctly observed that A defended inconvenience, not invisibility, all debate. Add the format note that A's first rebuttal was clipped for overrunning, and B holds the cleaner, still-live path.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's pressure question "what in this motion prevents passing both?" — A honestly conceded nothing does, converting its load-bearing crowd-out objection into a speculative sequencing claim, while B's paired line that every CON remedy (cause standard, human review, subpoenas) presupposes knowing an algorithm decided kept the precondition argument alive to the end.</best_rebuttal>
